narrative: The model estimates a 66% chance that you will leave your job. That is a high risk estimate—roughly two in three—not a certainty, but enough that the organization treats retention risk as a reason to deny the promotion now. The strongest signal pushing toward leaving is that you reported having other job opportunities while in this job; that is uncommon among employees predicted to stay, where about 77% had no such opportunities. The second strongest signal is your overall experience: you have 11+ years across jobs, while only about 15% of employees predicted to stay are in that bracket, so your broader experience may make outside moves more likely. The third signal is your sector being in the “other” category, which is somewhat less common among stayers and adds to the leave-side pressure. All three top factors push in the same direction: toward leaving rather than staying. Positive factors such as recognition, stability, and general job satisfaction are present, but they did not outweigh these retention-risk signals. Next, you and the organization should discuss what would make staying attractive: clearer promotion paths, concrete development opportunities, and a retention plan that addresses the external opportunities you see. The denial should be revisited if that risk is reduced.
